explanations.explanation: You got it, friend. Right after "It is for freedom that Christ has set us free," Paul says, "Stand firm, then" (Galatians 5:1). Freedom isn't something you set down on the counter and wander off from. You plant your feet and you STAY.

explanations.answer: Work hard to earn their freedom
explanations.explanation: Earn it? Friend, Paul says Christ already set them free: "It is for freedom that Christ has set us free" (Galatians 5:1). You can't pay for a gift that's already been handed to you. Paul's very next words are "Stand firm," so their job is to stand in it.

Keep quiet? This man wrote a whole LETTER about it! Paul tells them, "Stand firm, then, and do not be encumbered once more by a yoke of slavery" (Galatians 5:1). Nothing in there about hushing up. He tells them to stand, not to whisper.

That's right, baker. Paul says, "do not be encumbered once more by a yoke of slavery" (Galatians 5:1). Encumbered just means weighed down. And catch those two words, "once more." He doesn't want them picking that heavy thing back up.

It's true, friend. Paul's words are "do not be encumbered once more by a yoke of slavery" (Galatians 5:1), and encumbered means weighed down. Christ set them free, and going back under that yoke is what Paul warns against. That's like finally taking off a backpack full of bricks and saying, "You know what? I miss my bricks."
Paul doesn't soften it one bit: "Christ will be of no value to you at all" (Galatians 5:2). Not a little less. NONE. Those last two words, "at all," slam every door shut.

I see the thinking, friend. Add circumcision, get a bonus, right? But Paul says if they let themselves be circumcised, "Christ will be of no value to you at all" (Galatians 5:2). It doesn't add up to more. It goes straight to zero.

Same value would mean it makes no difference either way. But Paul says, "Christ will be of no value to you at all" (Galatians 5:2). That's not the same. That's a whole different number, and he signs his own name to it.

Paul says the opposite, friend. A man who gets himself circumcised "is obligated to obey the whole law" (Galatians 5:3). Not one command. The WHOLE thing. That's like clicking "free trial" and finding out you just signed up for the entire subscription, forever.

You read it right, baker. Paul says that man "is obligated to obey the whole law" (Galatians 5:3). One step in, and he's on the hook for every command. Paul even opens with "Again I testify," so this is a point he's making one more time.

explanations.answer: They have been severed from Christ
explanations.explanation: That's it. Paul says, "You who are trying to be justified by the law have been severed from Christ" (Galatians 5:4). Severed means cut off. I think Paul picks the strongest word he can find so nobody misses it.

explanations.answer: They have drawn closer to Christ
explanations.explanation: I can see how someone might think more rules means closer to Christ. But Paul says those trying to be justified by the law "have been severed from Christ" (Galatians 5:4). That's not closer. That's cut off.

Extra grace? Friend, grace isn't a rewards card where you rack up points at the register. Paul says those trying to be justified by the law "have fallen away from grace" (Galatians 5:4). No bonus points. They've fallen away from it.

Faith it is. Paul writes, "But by faith we eagerly await through the Spirit the hope of righteousness" (Galatians 5:5). Catch that little word "But." He just finished talking about people trying to be justified by the law, and then he turns the corner.

Law is the very thing Paul just warned about. He says those trying to be justified by the law "have fallen away from grace" (Galatians 5:4). Then comes the turn: "But by faith we eagerly await through the Spirit the hope of righteousness" (Galatians 5:5). Faith, friend.

Effort sounds right to a stamper like me. Back when my edges wore soft, Mother Miller, the lady I baked with for years, just pressed HARDER, and the cookies still came out blurry. Paul says, "But by faith we eagerly await through the Spirit the hope of righteousness" (Galatians 5:5). Faith, through the Spirit. Not elbow grease.

You got it, friend. Paul says, "What matters is faith expressing itself through love" (Galatians 5:6). In Christ Jesus, circumcision and uncircumcision have no value. Faith is what counts, and it shows up as love.

Keeping every command perfectly isn't what Paul points to here. He says, "What matters is faith expressing itself through love" (Galatians 5:6). Just a few verses back, he warned that the circumcised man "is obligated to obey the whole law" (Galatians 5:3). Paul isn't steering them toward that load.

explanations.answer: Coming from the right family line
explanations.explanation: Family line doesn't come up in this verse at all. Paul says, "What matters is faith expressing itself through love" (Galatians 5:6). Trust me, friend, I came out of a bargain bin with a 25 cent sticker on me, and nobody ever asked about my family tree. Faith and love, that's the list.

Paul says the opposite, friend. "Such persuasion does not come from the One who calls you" (Galatians 5:8). That's like a text claiming to be from your bank asking for your password. Look closer, and it's not the bank.
Right, baker. Paul writes, "Such persuasion does not come from the One who calls you" (Galatians 5:8). Whatever's slowing them down, it has a different source. The One who calls them isn't behind it.
The whole batch, friend. "A little leaven works through the whole batch of dough" (Galatians 5:9). A LITTLE. Small amount, and it reaches every corner of that dough.
Just the top? I wish it were that polite. Paul says, "A little leaven works through the whole batch of dough" (Galatians 5:9). Top to bottom. Edge to edge.

It doesn't stay put like that. Paul says, "A little leaven works through the whole batch of dough" (Galatians 5:9). It's like one person stirring things up in the group chat, and five minutes later all forty people are typing. The whole batch.
Exactly. "The one who is troubling you will bear the judgment, whoever he may be" (Galatians 5:10). Whoever he may be. Paul doesn't even need a name. Whoever it is, it lands on him.

explanations.answer: He will be let off free
explanations.explanation: Not a chance, friend. Paul says the one troubling them "will bear the judgment, whoever he may be" (Galatians 5:10). Nobody's getting waved through. And about the Galatians themselves, Paul says he's "confident in the Lord" that they will "take no other view."

explanations.answer: He will be put in charge
explanations.explanation: Put in CHARGE? That's like the guy who jams the copier getting promoted to head of the copy room. Paul says the one troubling them "will bear the judgment, whoever he may be" (Galatians 5:10). No promotion. Judgment.

I see why it reads that way, friend, but it's a question, not a confession. Paul asks, "if I am still preaching circumcision, why am I still being persecuted?" (Galatians 5:11). He IS still being persecuted, so the question points the other way. And if he were preaching it, he says, "the offense of the cross has been abolished."

You caught it, baker. Paul isn't owning up to anything. He's asking, "why am I still being persecuted?" and the answer is right there: he still is (Galatians 5:11). Then he says that if he were preaching circumcision, "the offense of the cross has been abolished."

That's right. Paul says, "do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh" (Galatians 5:13). That's like your boss saying you can work from home, and you hear "nap till noon." Freedom isn't a loophole, and Paul follows it with "Rather, serve one another in love."

It's true, friend. Paul writes, "you, brothers, were called to freedom; but do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh" (Galatians 5:13). Called to freedom, yes. But that freedom isn't a free pass for the flesh. Right after, he says, "Rather, serve one another in love."

You got it. Paul says the entire law is fulfilled in this one decree: "Love your neighbor as yourself" (Galatians 5:14). It goes all the way back to Leviticus 19:18. The whole law in one line, friend. That's the tightest packing job I've ever seen, and I pack cookie boxes all day.

The Sabbath is a real command, friend (Exodus 20:8). But it's not the one Paul names here. He says the entire law is fulfilled in a single decree, and it's "Love your neighbor as yourself" (Galatians 5:14). One decree carrying all of it.

Honoring your father and mother is a real command too (Exodus 20:12). But Paul points to a different one: "Love your neighbor as yourself" (Galatians 5:14). He says the entire law is fulfilled in that single decree. That's a lot riding on one line.

Consumed is the word. Paul warns, "But if you keep on biting and devouring one another, watch out, or you will be consumed by one another" (Galatians 5:15). Biting, devouring, consumed. He keeps that picture going right to the end.

Scattered isn't Paul's word here. He says, "watch out, or you will be consumed by one another" (Galatians 5:15). Ever leave a box of cookies in the break room at work? Nobody scatters. That box gets CONSUMED.
Shamed isn't the word Paul uses. He warns, "watch out, or you will be consumed by one another" (Galatians 5:15). Consumed, as in eaten up. It fits right with the biting and devouring just before it.
